highlights.title: CERA-MoA: Co-Evolving Routing Mechanisms with Continually Learning LLM Agents
highlights.summary: CERA-MoA introduces an iterative reinforcement‑learning framework where a dynamic router and LLM agents co‑evolve, using mid‑layer hidden states to estimate agent familiarity and adaptively activate a minimal set of agents.
highlights.detail: Previous Mixture‑of‑Agents pipelines treated routing and fine‑tuning as separate stages, limiting adaptation. CERA‑MoA’s predictive familiarity estimator avoids costly full rollouts by inspecting hidden activations. The cumulative‑threshold routing keeps the active agent pool small, enabling continual specialization after deployment. This design aims to improve overall system efficiency and responsiveness to evolving capabilities.

highlights.title: Infinite-Parameter LLMs: Generating and Adapting Weights from Live Data
highlights.summary: The paper proposes an architecture that can generate and adapt LLM weights on‑the‑fly from live user interactions, extending Mixture‑of‑Experts models beyond static pretraining.
highlights.detail: Current large language models freeze weights after training and rely on prompts to inject live information, which is discarded after each request. The proposed system treats user‑supplied facts and corrections as weight updates, allowing continual learning without retraining. This could reduce dependence on massive pretraining corpora and personalize behavior, though challenges remain around stability, latency, and security of on‑the‑fly weight generation.

highlights.title: Beyond Outcomes: Dual-View Relational Learning for Efficient Agent Benchmarking
highlights.summary: DualViewEval compresses agent benchmarks by jointly modeling outcome and process signals, achieving 24‑to‑40‑fold reduction while preserving score accuracy using only 20 tasks.
highlights.detail: Earlier compression methods focused solely on redundancy in final‑score distributions, ignoring rich process information. DualViewEval extracts six complementary trajectory signals and learns an exact‑size miniset that predicts full‑benchmark results. Tested on five agent benchmarks against five baselines, it consistently outperformed prior approaches, enabling faster evaluation of costly agent systems.

highlights.title: Upcoming: Codeforces Round (Div. 1)
highlights.summary: Codeforces Div. 1 round runs 2.5 hours, starting Saturday 26 Sep at 14:35 UTC.
highlights.detail: The contest is a Division 1 event, targeting top‑rated participants. It follows the standard Codeforces format with problems of increasing difficulty. The UTC start time helps global competitors plan their schedule. No registration is required beyond a Codeforces account.

highlights.title: A 3D Rasterizer For Embedded Devices
highlights.summary: A new 3D rasterizer implementation demonstrates that modern microcontrollers can render three‑dimensional graphics directly on embedded hardware.
highlights.detail: The rasterizer uses optimized fixed‑point arithmetic and leverages available hardware acceleration to fit within the limited RAM of typical ARM Cortex‑M devices. The open‑source code targets popular development boards, enabling hobbyists to create interactive 3D UI elements and visualizations on low‑cost platforms.

items.title: Helping older adults use AI in everyday life
items.summary: OpenAI and AARP are offering free, hands‑on ChatGPT workshops to 1,000 older adults in ten U.S. cities.
items.detail: The workshops aim to build practical AI skills safely, covering prompt engineering, privacy, and everyday use cases. Leveraging AARP’s senior network, sessions are scheduled over the coming months and are open to any older adult interested in exploring generative AI tools.

items.title: How to connect AI usage to business value
items.summary: OpenAI explains how ChatGPT Work and Codex analytics can surface AI usage patterns, spending, and training gaps to link adoption with business outcomes.
items.detail: The analytics suite provides per‑user and team metrics such as token consumption, frequent error types, and feature adoption rates. By identifying training needs and cost drivers, managers can justify ROI, allocate resources, and plan targeted upskilling programs.

items.title: How workers are unlocking new ways of working
items.summary: OpenAI’s Economic Research report reveals that workers are incorporating AI into non‑traditional tasks, creating recurring activities that reshape daily workflows.
items.detail: The study surveyed thousands of users across multiple industries, highlighting new AI‑driven activities like data cleaning, code generation, and content summarization. Findings show measurable productivity gains and the emergence of hybrid job functions, underscoring the need for upskilling and policy updates.

items.title: Fedora 45 beta drags the Linux console into the 21st century (Register)
items.summary: Fedora 45 beta swaps the legacy in‑kernel console for the kmscon userspace terminal emulator, modernizing text‑mode interaction.
items.detail: kmscon, in development for over a decade, offers better Unicode handling, configurable fonts, and easier debugging than the traditional console. The change affects all Fedora spins that rely on the console during boot and rescue, and may influence other distributions to adopt a similar userspace approach.

items.title: Security updates for Wednesday
items.summary: LWN reports a multi‑distribution security update rollout covering kernels, libraries, and services across AlmaLinux, Debian, Fedora, Oracle, Red Hat, SUSE, and Ubuntu.
items.detail: The updates address numerous CVEs in components such as OpenSSL, nginx, and Python. Administrators are urged to apply the patches promptly; the bulletin provides per‑distribution package lists and links to upstream advisories for detailed vulnerability information.

items.title: [$] LWN.net Weekly Edition for September 17, 2026
items.summary: The September 17 2026 LWN weekly edition covers server‑data encryption, PostgreSQL patches, faster kernel builds, BPF for blk‑iocost, and other community briefs.
items.detail: Highlights include new server‑side encryption APIs, a controversial PostgreSQL patch set fixing replication bugs, and performance improvements that reduce kernel compilation times. The edition also features a lessons‑learned article from a recent DPL and assorted announcements from the open‑source community.

items.title: [$] Ways to encrypt data on servers
items.summary: At FOSSY 2026, Romeo Solano presented practical approaches to encrypting server data, addressing threats like espionage and remote‑boot constraints.
items.detail: Solano discussed challenges of encrypting headless systems without keyboard access and reviewed solutions such as TPM‑based sealing, network‑bound disk encryption, and initramfs key retrieval. He emphasized trade‑offs between security guarantees and operational complexity for production environments.

items.title: A Cheap and Easy Control Screen For Home Assistant
items.summary: A low‑cost, DIY control screen design lets users operate Home Assistant directly from a dedicated display.
items.detail: The project combines a small LCD, a Raspberry Pi Zero, and open‑source software to render the Home Assistant UI. Assembly requires minimal soldering, and the screen can be wall‑mounted and powered via USB. All design files and firmware are hosted on GitHub for easy customization.

items.title: Zero-I/O Fault Recovery for Sharded Deep Learning via Dynamic Framework Dependency Rebinding
items.summary: AccelPact enables zero‑I/O in‑memory fault recovery for sharded distributed training, removing checkpoint overhead that previously added up to +656.7 % latency, used 32.5 GiB memory and generated 3.39 TB/h storage traffic.
items.detail: AccelPact keeps device memory quiescent after a communication failure, allowing training to resume without writing checkpoints to disk. It integrates with frameworks such as PyTorch FSDP by rebinding internal communication handles. By avoiding asynchronous snapshotting, it eliminates storage back‑pressure and reduces overall training time. The approach is transparent to the training code, requiring only runtime support.

items.title: AUPE: Collaborative byzantine fault-tolerant peer-sampling
items.summary: AUPE introduces the first collaborative Byzantine‑tolerant peer‑sampling protocol, improving resistance to malicious nodes that bias view composition.
items.detail: Existing Byzantine‑tolerant samplers lose effectiveness as the fraction of malicious nodes grows. AUPE lets honest participants share sampling information, counteracting attempts to inflate Byzantine representation in local views. The protocol maintains low overhead while providing stronger guarantees in permissionless blockchain settings. It is the first to combine collaboration with Byzantine fault tolerance in peer sampling.

items.title: Distribution-Aware Distributed Database Testing (Extended Version)
items.summary: DAT is an automated testing framework that leverages distribution‑aware information to generate queries exposing bugs specific to distributed database execution strategies.
items.detail: DAT captures logical schema definitions together with data‑distribution strategies (e.g., sharding, replication) and uses guided query mutation to provoke diverse execution paths. By focusing on distribution‑specific optimizations, it finds bugs that centralized test generators miss. The approach improves test executability and bug‑detection rates across multiple DDBMS implementations.

items.title: DiverseFT: Diversifying Fault-Tolerant Systems using LLMs
items.summary: DiverseFT uses large language models to automatically produce semantically diverse, compilable implementations of fault‑tolerant protocols, enabling scalable diversification of replica software.
items.detail: Given a reference implementation, DiverseFT prompts LLMs to generate alternative code that passes the original test suite while differing at the binary level. The generated variants reduce common‑mode failures caused by shared bugs. The system can be integrated into CI pipelines to continuously refresh replica diversity without manual coding effort.

items.title: Netkit: Specializing Linux Packet Delivery for Container Networks
items.summary: Netkit is an eBPF‑based datapath that specializes the Linux networking stack to skip redundant backlog queue traversals during container namespace transitions, boosting intra‑host container communication without code changes.
items.detail: Netkit inserts eBPF programs that directly redirect packets between network namespaces, eliminating unnecessary buffering in the Linux backlog queue. It preserves full compatibility with the standard Linux network stack, so existing containerized applications run unchanged. The implementation resides in the kernel and has been shown to reduce latency for same‑host container traffic.

items.title: RayOrch: Programming and Executing Lineage-Controlled Multi-Grain Dataflows for Foundation-Model Data Preparation
items.summary: RayOrch offers a programming model and distributed engine that preserves parent‑child lineage while batching variable‑cardinality expansions for foundation‑model data preparation.
items.detail: Developers declare ordered expansions of parent items into child records; the RayOrch compiler validates matching gather operations. At runtime, the system records each child's parent and ordinal position, enabling GPUs to batch children across many parents while respecting ordering constraints. This lineage awareness simplifies downstream processing of large, heterogeneous training datasets.

items.title: TencentCloud/Octop
items.summary: Octop is a self‑hosted, multi‑user, multi‑agent AI assistant designed for Tencent Cloud deployments.
items.detail: Octop runs on private infrastructure, allowing organizations to control data and model access. It supports multiple concurrent users and can orchestrate several specialized agents for tasks such as scheduling, retrieval, or code assistance. The project is open source and aims to provide a secure alternative to cloud‑based assistants.

items.title: Q00/ouroboros
items.summary: Ouroboros is an agent OS that autonomously evolves agents via interview‑gated, staged evaluation loops, supporting 14 runtimes such as Claude, Gemini, and Copilot.
items.detail: The system runs agents through a budgeted evolution loop where each iteration is screened by an interview process to ensure safety and alignment. It can invoke a wide range of LLM backends, providing flexibility for different tasks. The staged evaluation isolates regressions and enables controlled scaling of agent capabilities.

items.title: cline/cline
items.summary: cline provides an autonomous coding agent available as an SDK, IDE extension, or CLI assistant.
items.detail: cline can be embedded into development workflows to generate, refactor, or explain code on demand. It offers a command‑line interface for quick scripting and plugins for popular IDEs, enabling seamless interaction without leaving the editor. The agent operates locally, preserving code privacy.

items.title: JingMatrix/NeoZygisk
items.summary: NeoZygisk implements Zygote injection via ptrace for Android, enabling low‑level process manipulation.
items.detail: By attaching to the Zygote process with ptrace, NeoZygisk can inject custom code into newly spawned Android applications. This technique is useful for security research, custom ROM development, and runtime modification of system services without altering the Android framework binaries.

items.title: NVIDIA/cuda-quantum
items.summary: cuda‑quantum adds C++ and Python support for the CUDA Quantum programming model, facilitating heterogeneous quantum‑classical workflows.
items.detail: The library provides APIs that let developers write quantum kernels alongside CUDA code, targeting NVIDIA GPUs for simulation or hybrid execution. It abstracts hardware details, enabling rapid prototyping of quantum algorithms within familiar programming environments.

items.title: OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer
items.summary: OrcaSlicer is an open‑source C++ G‑code generator supporting major 3D printer families such as Bambu, Prusa, Voron, VzBot, RatRig, and Creality.
items.detail: The slicer produces printer‑specific G‑code from STL or OBJ models and offers configurable print settings, multi‑material handling, and preview visualizations. It is actively maintained on GitHub, allowing contributions and custom extensions. Its C++ codebase aims for high performance on typical desktop hardware.
